title: Inside the Unfair Judge: A Mechanistic Account of LLM-as-Judge Bias
hook: LLM judge bias isn't just noisy scoring — it has a geometric signature in hidden states you can find, steer, and use to predict failures on benchmarks you've never tested.
key_points: Across 7 judges, 7 bias types, and 9 benchmarks, biased inputs sit displaced along a low-dim, bias-type-specific subspace of hidden states.
This displacement sharpens with depth and is recovered consistently by three different estimation methods.
Steering hidden states along the subspace causally drives scoring both ways: inducing bias on clean inputs, or removing it from biased ones.
Random directions of matched size barely move the score, confirming the effect is specific to this subspace, not generic noise.
A linear projection onto the bias direction predicts judge failures on three unseen benchmarks, beating text-based bias detectors.
content_html: Most work on LLM-as-judge bias treats it as an input-output problem: perturb the prompt, watch the score move, patch it with better prompting. This paper looks inside the judge instead, and finds the bias has a consistent shape in its hidden states.
extra_html: Across seven judge models, seven bias types, and nine benchmarks, the authors find biased judging inputs occupy a displaced, low-dimensional subspace relative to the tight activation manifold that clean inputs sit on — a subspace specific to each bias type that sharpens in deeper layers, recovered consistently by three different estimation methods. Steering hidden states along this direction is causal: pushing forward reproduces biased scoring on clean inputs, pushing backward restores baseline scoring on biased ones, while random directions of the same size barely move the score at all. Practically, a simple linear projection onto the same bias direction anticipates judge failures on three benchmarks the projection never saw, beating text-based bias-detection baselines. Zixiang Xu and colleagues, arXiv 2026; project page at xzx34.github.io/unfair-judge.

related.title: Brand as Memory: VLMs Trust the Masthead, Not the Evidence
related.hook: Show a VLM the same article under a trusted outlet's logo versus an unknown one, and its verdict swings by 1.8x — a bias localized to three specific layers and steerable away.

related.title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate?
related.hook: LLM-as-a-Judge assumes evaluation is easier than generation — a controlled test finds the opposite on 3 of 4 benchmarks, and attention analysis shows why.

flashcards.prompt: Where does LLM-as-judge bias live, according to this paper's 'geometry' finding?
flashcards.back_html: In a low-dimensional, bias-type-specific subspace of the judge's hidden states — biased inputs are displaced along it, and the displacement sharpens with depth.

flashcards.prompt: How do the authors show the bias subspace is causal, not just correlational?

choices.text: Steering hidden states along it forces scoring in either direction, while random directions barely move scores
They retrain the judge from scratch without any biased examples
They ask the judge to explain its own reasoning in plain text

flashcards.explanation_html: Forward steering reproduces biased scoring on clean inputs; reverse steering restores baseline scoring on biased inputs — matched-norm random directions shift scores far less.

flashcards.prompt: What can the bias-direction projection do that text-based bias detectors can't match?
flashcards.back_html: Predict judge failures on three benchmarks never used to build it, substantially outperforming text-based (input-output) bias-detection alternatives.
